title: Genetics of Autism, ID & Encephalopathies
summary: The genetic architecture of autism, intellectual disability, developmental epilepsies and polygenic neurodevelopmental conditions.

lessons.title: Genetic Architecture of Autism

levels.kid:
Autism is a different way a brain can grow and work. Some autistic people notice tiny details, love patterns, or find loud noises and busy places hard. Others may talk late or not use many words.

Scientists study families and twins to learn why. They found that genes, the instruction book inside every cell, play a big part. There is not one "autism gene." Instead, hundreds of genes can each nudge brain building a little.

Think of baking a cake with a giant recipe. Sometimes one big change in the recipe matters a lot. More often, many tiny changes add up. Most of these changes are passed down in families. A few are brand new in the child. Nobody caused them, and vaccines do not cause autism.
levels.hs:
**Autism spectrum disorder (ASD)** is a neurodevelopmental condition defined by differences in social communication plus restricted, repetitive behaviors or interests. About 1 in 36 US children was identified with autism in CDC data from 2020, and boys are diagnosed roughly four times as often as girls.

**Heritability** is the share of differences in a trait across a population that is explained by genetic differences. Twin studies compare **identical twins** (who share nearly all their DNA) with **fraternal twins** (who share about half). Identical twins are far more often both autistic, and large studies estimate the heritability of autism at about 80%.

The genetic risk comes in two main forms:
- **Common variants**: DNA differences carried by many people. Each one has a tiny effect, but thousands of them together add up.
- **Rare variants**: uncommon changes, sometimes **de novo** (new in the child, not inherited). A single rare variant can have a large effect.

A real example: **fragile X syndrome**, caused by a repeat expansion in the gene **FMR1**, is the most common single-gene cause of autism. Many boys with fragile X meet autism criteria.

Genetic testing finds a specific cause in only about 10-20% of autistic people. For most, autism reflects many genes plus non-genetic factors. Large studies have firmly ruled out vaccines as a cause.
levels.college:
Autism's genetic architecture combines variants spanning a wide range of frequencies and effect sizes.

**Evidence for heritability**
- Twin concordance is much higher in monozygotic than dizygotic pairs. A 2016 meta-analysis (Tick et al.) estimated heritability at 64-91%.
- Swedish and five-country population cohorts (Sandin et al.) put heritability near 80%.
- Sibling recurrence is about 10-20%, many times the population rate. It is higher when the older affected sibling is a girl.

**Classes of variants**
- **Common SNPs**: SNP-based heritability is roughly 12-18%. GWAS (Grove et al., 2019) found the first five genome-wide significant loci.
- **Rare inherited variants**: these have moderate effects and often come from unaffected parents.
- **De novo variants**: these include protein-truncating SNVs and **copy-number variants (CNVs)**. Recurrent CNVs at 16p11.2, 15q11-13 duplications and 22q11.2 confer substantial risk. Sanders et al. (2011) showed that de novo CNVs are enriched in affected children compared with their unaffected siblings.
- **Syndromic monogenic causes**: fragile X (FMR1), tuberous sclerosis (TSC1/TSC2), PTEN hamartoma syndrome and Rett-spectrum MECP2 disorders.

**Convergent biology**
High-confidence genes cluster into two functional groups:
- **Synaptic function**: SHANK3, NRXN1, NLGN3/4X, SYNGAP1.
- **Gene-expression regulation**, including chromatin remodeling and transcription: CHD8, ARID1B, ADNP, POGZ.

These genes are expressed heavily in mid-fetal cortex, which points to prenatal development as a key window.

**Female protective effect**
Girls appear to need a greater genetic burden to become autistic. Affected females carry more de novo damaging variants on average, and their relatives show elevated autistic traits.

Clinically, chromosomal microarray and exome sequencing are recommended first-tier tests. They yield a diagnosis most often when autism co-occurs with intellectual disability.
levels.phd:
Autism risk is distributed across a continuum of allele frequency and penetrance. Liability-threshold modeling frames ASD as the tail of a normally distributed liability. Common variants shift the whole distribution, while rare variants of large effect push individuals across the threshold.

**Rare variant discovery.** Trio exome studies in the Simons Simplex Collection were pivotal. Iossifov et al. (2014) and De Rubeis et al. (2014) showed excess de novo likely gene-disrupting (LGD) variants in probands compared with siblings. TADA (Transmission And De novo Association) integrates de novo, inherited and case-control evidence. Satterstrom et al. (2020) identified 102 genes at FDR ≤0.1. Fu et al. (2022) extended this to 255 genes using more than 63,000 samples.

The yield depends on constraint. Damaging variants concentrate in genes intolerant of loss of function, measured by high pLI or low LOEUF. Haploinsufficiency is the dominant mechanism.

**Variant classes beyond coding SNVs**
- De novo CNVs explain several percent of simplex cases.
- Somatic mosaicism and noncoding de novo variants in promoters and enhancers have been proposed. Their contribution remains statistically weak despite large whole-genome efforts.
- Tandem repeat expansions are another emerging class.

**Common variation.** The iPSYCH-PGC GWAS (Grove et al., 2019; about 18,000 cases) found significant genetic correlations with educational attainment (positive), schizophrenia, depression and ADHD.

Polygenic transmission disequilibrium testing (Weiner et al., 2017) showed several things:
- Polygenic scores are over-transmitted to probands, but not to unaffected siblings.
- Common and rare risk act additively, not epistatically.
- Even carriers of high-impact de novo variants show polygenic over-transmission.

**The ASD-ID gradient.** Many top genes are associated more strongly with developmental delay than with autism specifically. Fu et al. separated genes with relatively greater ASD versus NDD enrichment. Probands with lower IQ carry more de novo LGD variants. Probands with higher IQ carry relatively more common-variant load.

**Convergence.** Co-expression analyses (Willsey et al., 2013; Parikshak et al., 2013) localize risk genes to mid-fetal deep-layer cortical projection neurons. Single-cell data implicate maturing excitatory and inhibitory neurons.

Several questions remain debated:
- Whether the female protective effect reflects genetic liability, phenotypic camouflaging or ascertainment bias.
- How much remaining heritability is truly missing.
levels.expert:
**Diagnostic genetics in practice.** Clinical yield varies sharply with phenotype:
- Chromosomal microarray finds a cause in about 7-9% of unselected autism cases.
- Exome sequencing finds a cause in about 15-20%.
- Yields rise with intellectual disability, dysmorphology, macro- or microcephaly, epilepsy or regression.

Genome sequencing increasingly replaces the stepwise approach. It captures CNVs, SNVs and some repeat expansions in a single assay. FMR1 repeat testing still needs a dedicated assay, because standard short-read pipelines miss the CGG expansion.

**Pitfalls**
- **Variable expressivity and incomplete penetrance.** A 16p11.2 deletion or NRXN1 deletion inherited from an unaffected parent does not exclude pathogenicity. Report these variants as susceptibility loci, not deterministic causes.
- **Variants of uncertain significance.** VUS outnumber pathogenic findings. Reclassification over time, and ancestry gaps in reference databases, create inequity in diagnostic yield.
- **Polygenic scores.** These explain only a few percent of liability and have no individual predictive value. Embryo or prenatal autism polygenic screening is scientifically unjustified and ethically contested.

**Why a molecular diagnosis matters.** It enables:
- Recurrence counseling. Siblings face about 1% risk for a confirmed de novo variant, allowing for gonadal mosaicism, versus up to 50% for an inherited dominant variant.
- Surveillance, such as tumor screening in PTEN syndromes and renal and cardiac imaging in TSC.
- Entry into patient registries and gene-specific trials.

**Toward precision therapy.** Lessons from mechanism-based trials temper expectations. mGluR5 antagonists, which rescued fragile X mice, failed in human trials. Outcome measures, age at treatment and placebo response were all implicated. mTOR inhibition with everolimus reduces TSC seizures, but has shown little cognitive benefit. Gene-dosage restoration is now the frontier:
- Antisense oligonucleotides for UBE3A in Angelman syndrome.
- Gene therapy for Rett syndrome, with a ceiling on MECP2 expression because duplication is also pathogenic.
- Trofinetide, approved in 2023 for Rett syndrome.

**Open questions**
- How brain-expressed noncoding variation contributes to risk.
- How environmental risk factors interact with genetic liability, for example prenatal valproate exposure and advanced paternal age, which is linked to increased de novo mutation.
- How to reconcile neurodiversity perspectives with research aimed at treatment. Many autistic adults prioritize support and co-occurring conditions such as epilepsy, anxiety and GI problems over core traits.

keyPoints: Autism heritability is roughly 80% from twin and population studies
Risk comes from common variants of tiny effect plus rare variants of large effect
De novo protein-truncating variants and CNVs (e.g. 16p11.2) are enriched in autistic children
Risk genes converge on synapses and chromatin/transcription regulation in mid-fetal cortex
Females appear to need a higher genetic burden (female protective effect)
Microarray and exome/genome sequencing find a cause in a minority, more with ID

They detect fragile X expansions too readily

lessons.title: Genetics of Intellectual Disability

levels.kid:
Your body is built from a giant instruction book called your **genes**. Some of those instructions tell the brain how to grow and how to learn.

Sometimes one tiny instruction has a typo. Then the brain may learn more slowly. Doctors call this **intellectual disability**. Kids with it can still learn, laugh, make friends and do lots of things. Learning just takes more time and help.

Often the typo is brand new. The parents did not have it. It happened by chance when the baby was starting to form. Nobody did anything wrong.

Today doctors can read a child's genes like proofreading a book. Finding the typo helps families understand why it happened. It also helps doctors give the best help.
levels.hs:
**Intellectual disability (ID)** means having significant limits in two areas: thinking skills, such as reasoning and problem-solving, and everyday **adaptive skills**, such as communicating and self-care. These limits must begin during childhood. ID affects roughly 1-2% of people.

Genes are a major cause, especially in more severe ID. Several kinds of genetic change can be involved:
- **Chromosome changes**: an extra or missing chromosome. **Down syndrome** (trisomy 21) is the most common genetic cause of ID.
- **Copy-number variants (CNVs)**: small missing or extra pieces of a chromosome.
- **Single-gene variants**: a change in one gene. Over 1,500 genes have been linked to ID.
- **X-linked causes**: genes on the X chromosome. **Fragile X syndrome** is the most common inherited single-gene cause. It is caused by an expanded CGG repeat in the *FMR1* gene.

A surprising finding is that many severe cases are caused by **de novo variants**. These are new mutations present in the child but not in either parent. This explains why ID often appears in families with no history of it.

Finding the cause matters. It ends the family's long search for a diagnosis and helps predict health problems. It also tells parents how likely it is to happen again in a future child.
levels.college:
ID is defined by deficits in intellectual functioning and adaptive behavior with onset in the developmental period (DSM-5). It is roughly split into **mild ID**, which is the most common, and **moderate-to-profound ID**. A useful rule is that more severe ID is more often **monogenic or chromosomal**. Mild ID more often reflects polygenic and environmental contributions.

**Classes of genetic cause:**
- **Aneuploidy**: trisomy 21 is the leading genetic cause overall.
- **CNVs**: examples include 22q11.2 deletion, Williams syndrome (7q11.23 deletion) and 1q21.1 deletion. **Chromosomal microarray** detects these and has a diagnostic yield of about 15-20% in unexplained ID.
- **Repeat expansion**: in Fragile X, more than 200 CGG repeats in the 5' UTR of *FMR1* cause hypermethylation and silencing. Without the gene there is no **FMRP**, an RNA-binding protein that represses local translation at synapses.
- **X-linked genes**: these partly explain why males are affected more often. *MECP2* (Rett syndrome) is one example.
- **Autosomal dominant de novo variants**: these are often loss-of-function. Examples include *SYNGAP1*, *ARID1B*, *DYRK1A* and *ANKRD11*.
- **Autosomal recessive genes**: these matter most in consanguineous populations.
- **Imprinting disorders**: Angelman syndrome is caused by loss of maternal *UBE3A*.

**Convergent biology.** ID genes cluster in a few functions:
- synaptic signaling (*SYNGAP1*, which encodes a Ras-GAP at the postsynaptic density)
- chromatin regulation (*ARID1B* in the BAF complex, *KMT2D*)
- transcription and translation control (mTOR pathway)

The testing approach has changed. Exome sequencing, with a yield of about 30-40%, is now recommended as a **first-tier test**. It can replace microarray as the first step or be paired with it.
levels.phd:
ID genetics illustrates **extreme genetic heterogeneity**. More than 1,500 genes are curated in SysID and Genomics England PanelApp, and most individual genes explain under 0.5% of cases. Two landmark studies reshaped the field. Vissers et al. (2010) used trio exome sequencing to show that **de novo point mutations** explain a large share of sporadic severe ID. Gilissen et al. (2014) used trio genome sequencing to reach a yield of about 62%. Since the per-generation de novo rate is about 1.2 × 10⁻⁸ per base, each child carries roughly 40-80 new variants. Distinguishing pathogenic hits requires statistics that compare observed with expected mutation counts per gene.

**Mutational constraint** is central. Genes intolerant of loss-of-function variants in gnomAD have high pLI or low LOEUF scores. These genes are heavily enriched for dominant ID. **Haploinsufficiency** dominates: a single working copy cannot sustain normal neurodevelopment. The large Deciphering Developmental Disorders (DDD) cohort, with more than 13,000 trios, found something more. Some genes act through **dominant-negative or gain-of-function** mechanisms. In these genes, missense variants cluster in specific domains rather than truncating variants spreading along the gene.

The DDD project also estimated something sobering. Even after all identified genes are counted, a large number of de novo ID genes remain undiscovered. Some recurrent causes also arise from **paternal age** through germline selfish selection.

Overlap with autism and epilepsy is substantial. Severe-effect de novo genes are shared across these conditions. Autism-predominant genes tend to be expressed in mature neurons, while ID-associated genes act earlier, in progenitors. Satterstrom et al. (2020) used this difference to separate genes with mainly ASD associations from those that act more generally in development.

Mild ID sits on the lower tail of a heritable cognitive distribution. **Polygenic scores** for educational attainment are lower in mild ID. Their contribution in severe ID is smaller but measurable. Common and rare variation can therefore combine in a liability model.

X-linked ID is the most historically mined category. Even so, the male excess is only partly explained by X-linked genes.
levels.expert:
Clinically, the evaluation of global developmental delay or ID follows ACMG (2021) guidance, which endorses **exome or genome sequencing as first-tier testing**. Genome sequencing adds detection of CNVs, structural variants, deep intronic and noncoding variants, and some repeat expansions in a single test. *FMR1* testing still requires a dedicated PCR and Southern blot or long-read assay, because short reads cannot size large CGG expansions.

**Pitfalls**
- **Variants of uncertain significance (VUS)**: missense VUS are common. Segregation, de novo status, phenotype match through GeneMatcher, and functional assays all help. The ACMG/AMP criteria must be applied rigorously.
- **Mosaicism**: parental low-level mosaicism raises the recurrence risk well above the roughly 1% usually quoted for an apparent de novo variant. A post-zygotic variant in the child may be missed in blood.
- **Dual diagnoses**: about 5% of solved cases have two molecular diagnoses, which produce blended phenotypes.
- **Reanalysis**: reinterpreting nondiagnostic exomes after 1-3 years adds a yield of roughly 10-15%, as gene discovery continues.

**Why diagnosis matters for treatment**
A molecular diagnosis can change management directly. Examples include:
- a creatine transporter or GAMT defect (creatine supplementation for GAMT)
- GLUT1 deficiency (ketogenic diet)
- cerebral folate deficiency
- inborn errors detected in parallel through metabolic screening

Recognizing a **mTORopathy** opens a path to targeted mTOR inhibition. Trials of **antisense oligonucleotides** are underway in Angelman syndrome. These ASOs unsilence the paternal *UBE3A* by targeting *UBE3A-ATS*. Fragile X trials teach caution. mGluR5 antagonists showed strong rescue in *Fmr1*-knockout mice but failed in humans. Possible reasons include outcome measures, the age at treatment and placebo response. This failure reshaped translational design.

**Open questions**
- the missing heritability in the many still-undiagnosed patients
- the role of noncoding and splicing variants
- critical windows: whether gene restoration later in life can recover cognition (Rett mouse models suggest substantial reversibility)
- equity: most reference datasets are European-ancestry, which lowers diagnostic yield in other populations

keyPoints: ID = limits in intellectual and adaptive function starting in childhood
Severe ID is more often monogenic or chromosomal; mild ID is more polygenic
Down syndrome is the top genetic cause; Fragile X is the top inherited single-gene cause
De novo, often haploinsufficient variants explain many sporadic severe cases
ID genes converge on synapses, chromatin and translation control
Exome/genome sequencing is now first-tier testing

advancedTest.explain: The biology held up in mice. Trial design factors such as outcome measures, the age at treatment and placebo response likely explain the human failure.

lessons.title: Dravet Syndrome and SCN1A

levels.kid:
Your brain has billions of tiny messenger cells called neurons. Some neurons are like gas pedals that say "go!" Others are like brakes that say "slow down!" A healthy brain needs both.

In **Dravet syndrome**, a tiny spelling mistake in one gene, called **SCN1A**, makes the brake neurons weak. Without good brakes, brain signals can race out of control. That causes **seizures**, which are like electrical storms in the brain.

The seizures usually start when a baby is less than one year old. Fevers or warm baths can set them off. Children with Dravet often learn more slowly as they grow.

Doctors use special medicines to help. Some old seizure medicines actually make Dravet worse, so knowing the gene helps doctors choose the right ones.
levels.hs:
**Dravet syndrome** is a severe genetic epilepsy that begins in the first year of life, usually around 6 months, in a baby who was developing normally. It is a **developmental and epileptic encephalopathy (DEE)**. That means the seizures and the genetic problem itself both interfere with brain development.

About 80-90% of patients have a mutation in **SCN1A**. This gene codes for **Nav1.1**, a **voltage-gated sodium channel**. Sodium channels are pores that let sodium ions rush into a neuron and fire an electrical signal called an action potential. Nav1.1 is especially important in **inhibitory interneurons**, which release the calming neurotransmitter **GABA**. When one copy of SCN1A is broken, these "brake" neurons cannot fire fast enough. The brain becomes overexcited.

Typical features:
- First seizures are often long, one-sided, and triggered by **fever** or heat
- Many seizure types appear later, plus long seizures called **status epilepticus**
- Development slows after age 1-2, with intellectual disability, autism features, and a crouched walking pattern
- Higher risk of **SUDEP** (sudden unexpected death in epilepsy)

Most mutations are **de novo**, meaning they are new in the child and not inherited from the parents.

A key example: **sodium channel-blocking drugs** like carbamazepine help many other epilepsies but worsen Dravet. They further silence the already-weak inhibitory neurons.
levels.college:
Dravet syndrome (formerly severe myoclonic epilepsy of infancy, SMEI) is caused in roughly 85% of cases by **heterozygous loss-of-function variants in SCN1A** (chromosome 2q24.3). Around 90% of these are de novo. About half are truncating (nonsense, frameshift, splice), and the rest are missense variants that are often in the pore region. Whole-gene deletions also occur.

**Mechanism: haploinsufficiency in interneurons.** Nav1.1 is the α-subunit of a voltage-gated sodium channel. It is enriched in **parvalbumin-positive fast-spiking interneurons**, and also in somatostatin and other GABAergic interneurons. These cells need large sodium currents to sustain high-frequency firing. With only 50% of normal Nav1.1, they fail during repetitive firing. Excitatory pyramidal neurons rely more on **Nav1.2 and Nav1.6**, so they are relatively spared. The result is network **disinhibition**.

**Why fever?** Nav1.1-deficient interneurons fail even more at higher temperatures. Hyperthermia reliably triggers seizures in Scn1a+/− mice.

**Clinical course:**
- Febrile and afebrile hemiclonic or generalized clonic seizures in infancy, often prolonged
- From ages 1-5, myoclonic, atypical absence, and focal seizures appear, along with status epilepticus, and development plateaus
- Later: intellectual disability, ADHD and autistic features, ataxia, crouch gait
- SUDEP and status-related death drive mortality, which is roughly 10-20% by adulthood

**Genotype-phenotype spectrum.** Milder SCN1A variants, sometimes missense and often inherited, cause **GEFS+** (genetic epilepsy with febrile seizures plus). Rare gain-of-function variants cause familial hemiplegic migraine type 3, or a distinct early-infantile DEE.

**Treatment principles.** Avoid sodium channel blockers (carbamazepine, oxcarbazepine, lamotrigine, phenytoin), because they aggravate seizures. Valproate and clobazam are first-line. Stiripentol, **fenfluramine** and **cannabidiol** have regulatory approval for Dravet based on randomized controlled trials. Families also use rescue plans for prolonged seizures.
levels.phd:
SCN1A encodes the 2009-residue Nav1.1 α-subunit. It has four homologous domains (DI-DIV), each with six transmembrane segments. S4 is the voltage sensor, and the S5-S6 loops form the selectivity filter. Claes et al. (2001) first identified de novo truncating SCN1A mutations in SMEI. That came after Escayg et al. (2000) linked SCN1A missense variants to GEFS+. The paradox that a sodium channel *loss* causes hyperexcitability was resolved by Yu et al. (2006, Catterall lab). In Scn1a+/− mice, sodium current fell in hippocampal GABAergic interneurons, while pyramidal neurons were unaffected. Cheah et al. (2012) then deleted Scn1a selectively in forebrain interneurons (Dlx1/2-Cre) and reproduced seizures and premature death. This established a cell-type-specific basis.

Later work refined the model:
- **PV interneurons** show depolarization block and impaired action-potential trains. **SST interneurons** contribute to network and behavioral phenotypes (Rubinstein et al.; Tai et al. 2014).
- **Developmental dynamics.** Favero et al. (2018) found that PV-interneuron deficits in Scn1a+/− mice partly normalize after the 3rd postnatal week. Persistent abnormalities remain in axon initial segment function and in other interneuron classes. This suggests the epileptic encephalopathy is not only a static current deficit.
- **Genetic background modifies severity.** Mouse phenotypes depend on strain: 129 versus C57BL/6 differ sharply, and modifier loci include Hlf and Cacna1g. This parallels the variable expressivity seen in human families.
- **Patient iPSC-derived neurons** have produced conflicting reports, some showing pyramidal hyperexcitability. This reflects differences in maturation state and culture systems.

Genotype-phenotype prediction is imperfect. Truncations and pore missense variants associate with Dravet. Milder missense variants associate with GEFS+. Mosaic parental variants explain some apparently "inherited" families. Variants in **SCN1B**, **GABRA1** and **PCDH19** can produce Dravet-like phenotypes. PCDH19 is X-linked with unusual female-limited expression through cellular interference.

Comorbidity is not simply a consequence of seizures. Interneuron-specific knockouts show cognitive and autistic-like deficits that can be partly separated from seizure burden. This supports the DEE concept, in which the developmental impairment is intrinsic to the mutation and not just secondary damage.
levels.expert:
**Diagnosis in practice.** Suspect Dravet when an infant has a prolonged, often hemiclonic febrile seizure before 12-15 months, followed by recurrent prolonged or vaccine- or fever-associated seizures, with a normal early EEG and MRI. Order an epilepsy gene panel or exome early, before developmental plateau. A positive result changes drug choice, prognosis counseling and trial eligibility. SCN1A testing should include copy-number analysis. Recurrence counseling must address parental mosaicism, found in roughly 5-10% of families. Berkovic et al. (2006) found SCN1A mutations in most patients with alleged pertussis-vaccine encephalopathy, reframing these cases as Dravet presentations. Vaccination did not change the outcome.

**Pitfalls:**
- Starting carbamazepine or lamotrigine for "focal seizures" before genetic results come back can precipitate status epilepticus
- Mislabeling early cases as complex febrile seizures delays diagnosis
- Adult patients are often undiagnosed. Their crouch gait, parkinsonian features and cognitive impairment may be attributed to other causes

**Pharmacology highlights.** Fenfluramine probably acts via serotonergic receptors, including 5-HT2C, and via σ1 receptor modulation, not appetite pathways. It requires echocardiographic monitoring for valvulopathy and pulmonary hypertension. Stiripentol inhibits CYP enzymes and potentiates GABA-A receptors, so interactions with clobazam matter. Cannabidiol also interacts with clobazam metabolism, raising its active metabolite N-desmethylclobazam.

**Disease-modifying advances.** Because the disease is haploinsufficiency, therapy aims to boost the healthy allele:
- **Zorevunersen (STK-001)** is an antisense oligonucleotide using TANGO technology. It blocks a poison exon (exon 20N) that triggers nonsense-mediated decay, raising productive SCN1A mRNA. It is given intrathecally. Phase 1/2 data showed reduced seizure frequency and possible cognitive and behavioral gains, and a phase 3 trial is under way.
- **ETX101** is an AAV9 vector carrying an engineered transcription factor. It upregulates endogenous SCN1A selectively in GABAergic interneurons, getting around the gene's ~6 kb size, which exceeds AAV capacity.

**Open questions:** Is there a critical window after which upregulation fails to rescue cognition? Can SUDEP risk, linked to brainstem and cardiac Nav1.1 dysfunction and post-ictal respiratory arrest, be predicted and prevented? How should trials measure non-seizure outcomes, such as adaptive behavior and sleep?

keyPoints: Dravet syndrome is a severe developmental and epileptic encephalopathy beginning in infancy
About 85% of cases are caused by de novo heterozygous loss-of-function SCN1A variants
SCN1A encodes Nav1.1, which is critical for fast-spiking GABAergic interneurons
Haploinsufficiency in interneurons causes network disinhibition, and fever is a classic trigger
Sodium channel blockers worsen seizures; fenfluramine, stiripentol and cannabidiol are approved
Antisense therapies such as zorevunersen aim to upregulate the healthy SCN1A allele

lessons.title: SCN2A, KCNQ2 and STXBP1 Encephalopathies

levels.kid:
Your brain cells talk using tiny electric signals. To make those signals, each cell has little **gates** in its skin that let charged particles in and out.

Some gates help start a signal, like a gas pedal. Other gates calm the cell down, like brakes. There are also helpers that let cells pass messages to each other, like a mail carrier.

Sometimes a baby is born with a tiny spelling change in the instructions for one of these parts. If the gas pedal sticks, or the brakes are weak, or the mail carrier is missing, the brain can get too excited. That can cause **seizures**, which are like electrical storms.

Doctors read the baby's genes to find which part is broken. Then they can choose the best medicine for that part.
levels.hs:
A **developmental and epileptic encephalopathy (DEE)** is a condition where seizures begin early, often in the first months of life, and development is also affected. Many DEEs are caused by a single **de novo** mutation, meaning a new change in the child's DNA that neither parent carries.

Three important genes:
- **SCN2A** makes a **sodium channel** (Nav1.2). Sodium rushing in starts the electrical signal in a neuron. Some mutations make the channel too active (**gain of function**). Others make it work too little (**loss of function**).
- **KCNQ2** makes part of a **potassium channel** that acts like a brake. Potassium flowing out helps calm the neuron. When KCNQ2 is weakened, neurons fire too easily.
- **STXBP1** makes a protein needed to release **neurotransmitters**, the chemical messages between neurons.

One real example: a baby with a SCN2A gain-of-function mutation may have seizures within the first days of life. Drugs that block sodium channels can help this baby a lot. But in a child with a loss-of-function SCN2A mutation, which often causes later seizures or autism, the same drugs can make seizures worse.

This is why **genetic testing** matters. The gene, and even the type of mutation, changes which treatment a doctor chooses.
levels.college:
Developmental and epileptic encephalopathies (DEEs) are disorders in which both epileptic activity and the underlying genetic defect impair development. Most are caused by heterozygous de novo variants in genes controlling neuronal excitability or synaptic function.

**SCN2A (Nav1.2).** This voltage-gated sodium channel α subunit sits mainly in the axon initial segment of excitatory neurons early in development. Later, Nav1.6 (SCN8A) partly replaces it there, and Nav1.2 also helps backpropagate action potentials into dendrites.
- **Gain-of-function** variants (enhanced current, slowed inactivation) cause **neonatal or early-infantile onset** seizures, before about 3 months. Phenotypes range from self-limited familial neonatal-infantile seizures to severe DEE. Sodium channel blockers such as phenytoin and carbamazepine often help.
- **Loss-of-function** variants (truncations, nonconducting channels) are strongly linked to **autism and intellectual disability**, sometimes with later-onset seizures. Sodium channel blockers are usually unhelpful or harmful.

**KCNQ2 (Kv7.2).** Kv7.2 and Kv7.3 subunits form the **M-current**, a slowly activating, non-inactivating potassium current that stabilizes resting potential and limits repetitive firing.
- Mild loss of function causes **self-limited familial neonatal epilepsy** (inherited, remits).
- De novo **dominant-negative** missense variants cause **KCNQ2-DEE**: seizures in the first week, often with tonic features and burst-suppression EEG, followed by developmental impairment.
- Sodium channel blockers, particularly carbamazepine, are often effective.

**STXBP1 (Munc18-1).** This protein binds syntaxin-1 and is essential for SNARE complex assembly and synaptic vesicle fusion.
- Variants are mostly **loss of function / haploinsufficiency**. They destabilize the protein so that less of it is present.
- They cause early-onset epilepsy, often infantile spasms or Ohtahara syndrome, along with ID, movement disorders and tremor. Some patients have ID with little or no epilepsy.

The key lesson is that **genotype and functional effect guide therapy**, not seizure type alone.
levels.phd:
These three genes show three different routes to a DEE: sodium-channel dysfunction, failure of the M-current brake, and failure of the presynaptic release machinery.

**SCN2A biophysics and cell type.** Nav1.2 is concentrated in excitatory pyramidal neurons and is the dominant initial-segment channel perinatally. This explains why GoF variants produce early-onset seizures. Patch-clamp studies of variants such as L1342P and R1882Q show hyperpolarized activation, impaired fast inactivation or increased persistent current. Ben-Shalom et al. (2017) showed that age of seizure onset tracks with the direction of the functional effect. GoF variants cluster in voltage-sensor and inactivation regions, whereas truncating variants are distributed along the gene. The phenotype of LoF variants is paradoxical: some Scn2a-haploinsufficient mice show cortical hyperexcitability. Spratt et al. (2021) proposed that loss of dendritic Nav1.2 weakens activation of somatodendritic potassium channels, so the neuron fires more. Developmental reduction of Nav1.2 is therefore not simply 'less excitability.'

**KCNQ2 and the M-current.** Kv7.2/7.3 heterotetramers are localized to the AIS and nodes via ankyrin-G binding. Their opening requires PIP2 and they are suppressed by muscarinic Gq signalling. Benign familial variants reduce current by about 25%, consistent with haploinsufficiency. DEE variants, such as those in the S4 voltage sensor, the pore, or PIP2/calmodulin-binding sites, often act dominant-negatively and reduce current far more. Rare KCNQ2 GoF variants (e.g., R201C/H) cause a distinct phenotype with neonatal encephalopathy without typical seizures, so here too direction of effect matters. Early GABAergic depolarization may make neonatal circuits especially reliant on the Kv7 brake.

**STXBP1 and haploinsufficiency.** Munc18-1 clasps closed syntaxin-1 and templates SNARE zippering. Guiberson et al. and Kovacevic et al. (2018) showed that many missense variants cause thermal instability and aggregation, with some co-aggregating wild-type protein. This raised a debate between pure haploinsufficiency and dominant-negative effects. The reduced protein levels support the use of chemical chaperones (e.g., 4-phenylbutyrate) in model systems. Inhibitory synapses may be disproportionately affected, which would tip network balance toward excitation.
levels.expert:
**Diagnostic yield and timing.** In neonatal-onset epilepsy with normal neuroimaging, gene panels or exome sequencing frequently identify KCNQ2, SCN2A, STXBP1 or KCNQ3 as the cause. Rapid genome sequencing in the NICU can return results within days and change treatment immediately. Pitfalls include classifying a missense variant without functional data, mosaicism in an apparently unaffected parent (which raises recurrence risk above the de novo baseline), and assuming phenotype from gene alone.

**Therapeutic stratification.**
- **SCN2A GoF**: early, often high-level sodium channel blockade can be dramatically effective. Overlap with SCN8A means similar logic.
- **SCN2A LoF**: avoid reliance on sodium channel blockers. Management targets autism, ID and later seizures. Antisense approaches to upregulate the remaining allele, or CRISPRa-based enhancement of Scn2a (Tamura et al. 2022), have rescued features in mice.
- **SCN2A GoF ASOs**: elsinersen (PRAX-222), an allele-agnostic antisense oligonucleotide that knocks down SCN2A, is in trials. Individualized ASOs have been given to single patients.
- **KCNQ2-DEE**: carbamazepine or other sodium channel blockers are first-line choices in many centres. Kv7 openers are logical. Ezogabine (retigabine) was withdrawn for retinal and skin pigmentation, and newer openers such as XEN1101 (azetukalner) are being studied. For KCNQ2 GoF encephalopathy, openers are mechanistically contraindicated.
- **STXBP1**: no disease-specific therapy is approved. Trials of 4-phenylbutyrate and gene-replacement programmes reflect haploinsufficiency logic.

**Outcome measures.** Seizure freedom does not equal developmental normalization: the 'encephalopathy' is partly genetic, independent of seizures. Trials increasingly use developmental and motor endpoints, caregiver-reported outcomes and EEG biomarkers. Natural-history registries (e.g., for STXBP1 and SCN2A) are essential because phenotypes are heterogeneous.

**Open questions.** Key questions remain about critical developmental windows for intervention, why identical variants produce variable severity (genetic background, modifiers), how to predict variant function computationally at scale, and how safe chronic intrathecal ASO delivery is in infants.

keyPoints: DEEs combine early seizures with developmental impairment, often from de novo variants
SCN2A gain-of-function causes early neonatal seizures responsive to sodium channel blockers
SCN2A loss-of-function links to autism/ID; sodium channel blockers can worsen it
KCNQ2 encodes Kv7.2, part of the M-current potassium 'brake'
STXBP1 (Munc18-1) is needed for vesicle fusion; variants cause haploinsufficiency
Functional effect of the variant, not just the gene, guides precision therapy

lessons.title: Polygenic Risk in ADHD and Schizophrenia

levels.kid:
Some things about you come from one big gene switch, like a single light switch that turns a room on or off. But many things, like how tall you grow, come from thousands of tiny switches. Each one only nudges a little bit.

ADHD and schizophrenia are brain conditions that work like the tiny-switch kind. ADHD can make it hard to sit still or focus. Schizophrenia can make it hard to tell what is real. Lots of small gene differences add up, and things in a person's life matter too.

No single tiny switch decides anything. Scientists study huge groups of people, sometimes hundreds of thousands, to find these small switches. That helps them understand how the brain works and find new medicines one day.
levels.hs:
Many traits are **polygenic**, meaning they are shaped by thousands of genetic variants that each have a very small effect. ADHD (attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder) and schizophrenia are classic examples.

Key ideas:
- **Heritability** is the share of differences between people in a group that is explained by genetic differences. Twin studies put it at about 70-80% for both ADHD and schizophrenia. That does not mean genes decide a person's fate.
- A **GWAS** (genome-wide association study) compares the DNA of hundreds of thousands of people with and without a condition. It scans millions of common variants called **SNPs** (single-nucleotide polymorphisms).
- A **polygenic risk score (PRS)** adds up a person's risk variants, each weighted by its effect size, into one number.

Real example: in 2014 the Psychiatric Genomics Consortium found 108 regions of the genome linked to schizophrenia. One of the strongest signals sat in the MHC region, an area best known for immune genes. Later work traced part of it to a gene called **C4**, which helps the brain prune its synapses (the connections between neurons). By 2022 the number of regions had grown to 287.

PRS can show who is at higher risk *on average*. They are not yet good enough to diagnose any single person. Environment matters too: for schizophrenia, cannabis use and childhood adversity add to risk.
levels.college:
ADHD and schizophrenia sit at the polygenic end of the genetic spectrum, unlike the monogenic encephalopathies covered earlier in this unit.

**Heritability estimates**
- Twin heritability is about 74% for ADHD and about 79-80% for schizophrenia.
- **SNP-heritability** is the part captured by common variants measured in GWAS. It is much lower: roughly 14% for ADHD and about 24% on the liability scale for schizophrenia.
- The gap is called **missing heritability**. Proposed sources include rare variants, imperfect tagging of causal variants, non-additive effects and inflated twin estimates.

**GWAS milestones**
- Schizophrenia: PGC 2014 reported 108 loci. Trubetskoy et al. (*Nature* 2022), with about 76,000 cases, reported 287 loci. Fine-mapped genes are enriched for expression in neurons and for synaptic biology, for example *GRIN2A*, *SP4* and *CACNA1C*.
- ADHD: Demontis et al. (*Nature Genetics* 2019) reported the first 12 genome-wide loci, including near *FOXP2*. Their 2023 analysis, with about 38,700 cases, raised this to 27 loci.
- Individual SNPs have tiny effects, with odds ratios typically around 1.05-1.1.

**Polygenic risk scores**
- A PRS is the sum of risk alleles, each weighted by its GWAS effect size.
- Schizophrenia PRS explains about 7-10% of variance in liability in European-ancestry samples. People in the top centile have roughly 3-5 times the odds of people at the median.
- **Genetic correlation**, estimated with LD score regression, reveals shared genetic architecture. ADHD correlates genetically with major depression and low educational attainment. Schizophrenia correlates strongly with bipolar disorder (rg about 0.7).

**Rare variants matter too.** The SCHEMA study (2022) found ultra-rare protein-truncating variants in 10 genes that raise schizophrenia risk sharply, among them *SETD1A*, *GRIN2A* and *CUL1*. Copy-number variants such as 22q11.2 deletion also confer high risk. The architecture therefore spans common and rare variants.
levels.phd:
Liability-threshold models frame both disorders as the tail of a continuous, normally distributed liability. Thousands of additive variants contribute, and diagnosis occurs above a threshold. Supporting this, ADHD PRS associate with dimensional inattention and hyperactivity in population samples. This fits evidence that ADHD is the extreme of a continuous trait.

**Schizophrenia biology from GWAS.** The MHC signal was dissected by Sekar et al. (*Nature* 2016). Structurally diverse *C4A/C4B* alleles predict *C4A* expression, and higher predicted *C4A* expression associates with risk. In mice, C4 mediates complement-tagged synaptic pruning. This links the signal to the observed reduction in dendritic spines and to adolescent onset, coinciding with late synaptic elimination. In PGC3, fine-mapping used SuSiE and FINEMAP alongside SMR and eQTL colocalization, prioritizing 120 genes. Enrichment analyses implicate excitatory and inhibitory neurons rather than glia. Convergence between common-variant (*GRIN2A*, *SP4*) and SCHEMA rare-variant signals supports NMDA-receptor hypofunction and glutamatergic synapse models over a pure dopamine account.

**ADHD.** Loci include *FOXP2*, *SORCS3* and *DUSP6*. In the 2023 study, risk genes showed enriched expression in midbrain dopaminergic neurons and frontal cortex during development. Candidate-gene findings, such as the *DAT1* and *DRD4* VNTRs, mostly failed to replicate at genome-wide significance. This was a cautionary chapter about small, underpowered samples.

**Pleiotropy.** The Cross-Disorder Group (*Cell* 2019) analyzed eight psychiatric disorders and found 109 pleiotropic loci. They resolved three factors: compulsive, mood/psychotic and early-onset neurodevelopmental, with ADHD and autism loading together. Genomic SEM yields a partial 'p-factor'.

**Nuances.**
- Within-family GWAS shrink effects for education-related traits, showing that population estimates include indirect genetic effects (genetic nurture), assortative mating and stratification. ADHD estimates attenuate modestly.
- Selection signatures are weak despite reduced fecundity in schizophrenia. This poses an evolutionary puzzle, partly explained by mutation-selection balance of rare variants.
- Mendelian randomization claims, such as cannabis causing schizophrenia, are confounded by bidirectional signals and horizontal pleiotropy.
levels.expert:
**Clinical utility of PRS remains limited.** The area under the curve for schizophrenia PRS is about 0.70 in European ancestry, which is inadequate for screening low-prevalence disorders. Positive predictive value stays low even in the top centile, because base rates are about 1%. Embryo selection on psychiatric PRS is offered commercially. Professional societies, including ESHG and ASHG statements, consider it unvalidated. The expected gains are small because sibling PRS variance is half the population variance. Pleiotropy also creates trade-offs: schizophrenia PRS correlates positively with creativity and some cognitive measures.

**Ancestry bias.** Most discovery cohorts are of European descent. PRS accuracy drops roughly 2-5-fold in African-ancestry samples because LD structure and allele frequencies differ. Multi-ancestry methods (PRS-CSx) and East Asian schizophrenia GWAS (Lam et al. 2019) help, but equitable performance is unsolved. Deploying scores clinically risks widening disparities.

**Research uses where PRS earn their keep:**
- Stratifying clinical high-risk cohorts. PRS adds modestly to transition prediction beyond symptoms (NAPLS, PSYSCAN).
- Treatment-resistance research. Higher schizophrenia PRS and rare-variant burden show weak associations with clozapine eligibility. Pharmacogenomic GWAS of clozapine-induced neutropenia point to *ACKR1* (the Duffy-null genotype). This matters clinically because Duffy-null benign neutropenia can otherwise lead to unnecessary discontinuation.
- Drug-target triage. Genetically supported targets are roughly twice as likely to succeed in trials, which motivates interest in complement and glutamatergic pathways. Muscarinic agonism (xanomeline-trospium, FDA-approved 2024) illustrates a non-D2 mechanism, though one not derived from GWAS.

**Pitfalls in reading studies:**
- Sample overlap between discovery and target cohorts inflates PRS performance.
- Ascertainment, such as clinic cases or population registries like iPSYCH, shifts the genetic signal. Registry ADHD cases with comorbidity carry heavier rare CNV burden.
- Collider bias in UK Biobank follows from its healthy-volunteer participation.

**Open questions:**
- Whether omnigenic models, in which peripheral genes act through core networks, apply to these disorders.
- Translating 287 loci into cell-type mechanisms with massively parallel reporter assays and CRISPR screens in iPSC-derived neurons.
- Integrating PRS with rare variants and environment, such as obstetric complications and urbanicity, into calibrated, ancestry-robust risk models, and deciding whether returning such results ever benefits patients.

keyPoints: ADHD and schizophrenia are highly heritable but polygenic: thousands of tiny-effect variants
Twin heritability is about 70-80%; SNP-heritability is much lower (missing heritability)
Schizophrenia GWAS grew from 108 loci (2014) to 287 (2022); ADHD reached 27 loci (2023)
The MHC signal partly reflects C4A and complement-mediated synaptic pruning
A polygenic risk score sums weighted risk alleles but cannot diagnose individuals
Rare variants (SCHEMA genes, CNVs) and environment add to common-variant risk

test.q: What does it mean that ADHD is polygenic?
choices: It is caused by one dominant gene
It results from a missing chromosome
Many variants each add a small effect
It is inherited through the mother
test.explain: Polygenic conditions are shaped by thousands of variants of small effect, unlike monogenic disorders driven by a single gene.

test.q: Twin-study heritability of schizophrenia is approximately:
test.explain: Twin studies estimate schizophrenia heritability at roughly 79-80%.

test.q: How many schizophrenia loci did the 2022 PGC study report?
test.explain: Trubetskoy et al. 2022 reported 287 loci. 108 was the 2014 figure, and 12 and 27 are the ADHD loci counts.

test.q: Which gene in the MHC region is linked to schizophrenia through synaptic pruning?
test.explain: Higher predicted C4A expression raises risk, and C4 tags synapses for complement-mediated pruning.

test.q: The gap between twin heritability and SNP-heritability is called:
test.explain: Missing heritability is the gap between twin estimates and the heritability captured by common SNPs.

test.q: Why can't a polygenic risk score yet diagnose an individual?
choices: It requires a brain biopsy sample
It measures one gene at a time
test.explain: PRS shifts average risk but explains only a modest share of variance, so individual prediction is poor.

test.q: Schizophrenia shows a strong genetic correlation (about 0.7) with:
test.explain: Schizophrenia and bipolar disorder share much of their common-variant architecture.

test.q: The SCHEMA study found that schizophrenia risk rises sharply with:
test.explain: SCHEMA identified ultra-rare protein-truncating variants in 10 genes, such as SETD1A, that confer large effects.

test.q: A typical single GWAS hit for these disorders has an odds ratio around:
test.explain: Individual common variants have tiny effects. Large odds ratios belong to rare variants and CNVs.

test.q: What is the abbreviation for a study that scans millions of SNPs across many people to find disease-linked regions?
test.explain: A genome-wide association study compares variant frequencies in cases and controls.

test.q: A polygenic risk ___ sums a person's risk alleles weighted by their effect sizes.
test.explain: The polygenic risk score (PRS) is a weighted sum of risk alleles.

test.q: What abbreviation names the common single-letter DNA variants measured in GWAS?
test.explain: Single-nucleotide polymorphisms are the common variants genotyped in GWAS.

kidTest.q: ADHD and schizophrenia come from:
choices: A cold virus caught in early childhood
A single gene mutation from one parent
kidTest.explain: Many small gene differences add up, along with life experiences.

kidTest.q: ADHD can make it hard to:
kidTest.explain: ADHD affects attention and activity.

kidTest.q: How do scientists find these tiny gene switches?
kidTest.explain: Very large studies are needed to spot such small effects.

kidTest.q: Does one tiny switch decide if you get schizophrenia?
choices: Yes, if you are an adult
kidTest.explain: Each tiny switch has a very small effect.

kidTest.q: Tiny instructions inside your body that come from your parents are called g _ _ _ s.
kidTest.explain: Genes carry instructions for building the body and brain.

advancedTest.q: Even top-centile schizophrenia PRS has low positive predictive value mainly because:
choices: PRS leave out the MHC region
Twin heritability is close to zero
The disorder's base rate is near 1%
GWAS loci cluster in immune genes
advancedTest.explain: With low prevalence, even a 3-5x odds increase yields mostly false positives.

advancedTest.q: Why does PRS accuracy drop in African-ancestry samples?
choices: Its LD and allele frequencies differ
Rare variants are absent in those genomes
Fewer risk genes exist in that ancestry
advancedTest.explain: Discovery GWAS are mostly European, and tagging SNPs and frequencies transfer poorly across ancestries.

advancedTest.q: The failure of DAT1 and DRD4 candidate-gene findings to replicate in GWAS mainly illustrates:
choices: That dopamine is irrelevant to ADHD
That ADHD is a monogenic disorder
advancedTest.explain: Small candidate-gene studies produced unreliable associations; well-powered GWAS did not confirm them.

advancedTest.q: Convergence of GRIN2A in both common- and rare-variant schizophrenia studies best supports:
choices: Mechanisms driven by glia, not neurons
A pure dopamine excess model of psychosis
advancedTest.explain: GRIN2A encodes an NMDA receptor subunit, and convergence across variant classes strengthens glutamatergic models.
